::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

table.title: Possible & Impossible Representations
table.research_questions:
Studies that assess children’s ability to deploy possibility concepts using a Y-shaped tube task – which require a child to catch a marble falling down a forked tube by covering both possible exits of tube — suggest that 3-year-olds generally deploy possibility concepts when choosing their actions (e.g., Andreuceolli et al., 2024; Redshaw & Suddendorf 2016). Others have argued that success in the Y-shaped tube task is better explained on the hypothesis that participants deploy “minimal representation of possibility” (Leahy & Carey 2020; Leahy et al. 2022). On this view, children use simulation to identify one location for a reward, and instead of marking that simulated location as merely possible, they take it to be the fact of the matter.
In one test of this idea, Leahy (2024) assessed children’s performance on a modified Y-shaped tube with two possible exits, where a third “impossible tube” was attached to the apparatus. Leahy reasoned that (1) a child who deploys minimal representations of possibility should cover one possible exit; (2) a child who is not evaluating the structure of the tube should often cover the impossible exit; and (3) a child who deploys possibility concepts should cover both possible exits. In this study, only 17% of 3-year-olds deployed possibility concepts (i.e., identified multiple incompatible possibilities while ruling out impossibilities by placing their hands under both ends of the Y-shaped tube).
In a further test of this hypothesis, the proposed study will examine whether children are minimal representers of possibility by making two modifications to Leahy’s (2024) procedure. First, instead of asking children to use their hands to catch dropping marbles, objects will fall into one of three opaque boxes. Two of these boxes will be connected to a Y-shaped tube, and a third box will be connected to a single (“impossible”) tube. On critical trials, children will be asked to identify two boxes they want to look inside by placing 1 sticker on each of them, and critically, will not be permitted to look inside any boxes until both choices are made (to preclude feedback that might allow a sequential simulation of possibilities). Second, the single tube will not be connected to the Y-shaped apparatus to account for potential failures in children’s knowledge of tube structure (i.e., to avoid the inference that the impossible arm is a viable option since it’s connected to the Y-shaped tube).
Our reasoning is that asking children to place stickers will force them to always make two choices, unlike studies that ask children to use their hands and allow them to choose their own strategy. One possibility, for example, is that modal reasoners understand that there are two possible exits for a ball, but prefer to place only one hand under their preferred “bet” of where it will emerge. We reasoned that when forced to make two choices (1) a child who deploys possibility concepts should cover both possible exits; and (2) a child who deploys minimal representations of possibility should choose one possible exit, and may choose randomly between the other two exits. Therefore, if children are minimal representers, and only succeed on Y-shaped tubes via sequential simulation, then they should fail in the present study since they do not have evidence that their initial choice is only merely possible.

table.title: Possible and Impossible Representations
table.research_questions:
In Study 1, we examined whether children are minimal representers of possibility on a modified version of Leahy’s (2024) impossible tubes task. First, instead of asking children to use their hands to catch dropping marbles, objects were dropped into one of three opaque boxes. Two of these boxes were connected to a Y-shaped tube, and a third box was connected to a single (“impossible”) tube. On critical trials, children were asked to identify two boxes they want to look inside by placing 1 sticker on each of them, and critically, were not be permitted to look inside any boxes until both choices were made (to preclude feedback that might allow a sequential simulation of possibilities). We found that the older children in our study (i.e., children between 31 and 38 months) almost always covered both possible exits, whereas younger children (i.e., children between 24 and 30 months) chose randomly between possible and impossible exits. The results of Experiment 1 indicated not just that children’s representations of possibility emerge gradually between 2 and 3 years of age, but critically, that 3-year-olds do deploy possibility concepts, contradicting the findings of previous studies.

In this follow-up study, we seek to replicate this pattern of findings, while removing children’s ability to adapt a heuristic while completing critical trials. In particular, we will address the possibility that older children might always choose both ends of the y-shaped tube when it is implicated in a trial (i.e., both when it is the right answer and when it is not). To do so, we will introduce an equal number of trials in which the correct answer is (a) both ends of the y-shaped tube (critical; see 4a), and (b) the impossible tube and one of the two y-shaped tubes (two-ball; see 4d). Therefore, if children are minimal representers, and only succeed on Y-shaped tubes by adapting a heuristic, then they should always choose the y-shaped tube, regardless of the correct choice. However, if children are distinguishing merely possible and impossible events, then we should see (1) continued success on the critical trial, and (2) a higher proportion of correct responses on both (critical and two-ball) trials relative to incorrect responses on both trials.

text.text: A prominent hypothesis in the literature on logical reasoning suggests that, unlike human adults and older children, 3-year-olds deploy a "minimal representation of possibility" when reasoning about the existence of a reward in one of two possible locations.

On this view, children are unable to represent two mutually exclusive possibilities simultaneously, and instead commit to one location for the reward in a pair of possible locations, only considering the second location once they have evidence that their first choice is not correct.

Although this hypothesis may explain children's struggles on various tests of modal reasoning, the idea that children may represent possible reward locations sequentially (rather than simultaneously) has not been directly tested.
In two studies, we asked 24-to 38-month-olds to choose two of three reward locations, one of which was physically impossible.
We found that children aged 31 to 38 months selected the two possible locations without feedback when required to make a simultaneous choice.
We argue that these data are compatible with an ability to represent multiple mutually exclusive possibilities.
The capacity to represent possibilities is central to human reasoning (Carey et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The capacity to represent possibilities is central to human reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Carey et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: People consider multiple outcomes when we make everyday decisions -e.g., whether to drive or take the bus to work, whether to cook dinner at home or order takeout, etc.

On some views, the ability to represent possibilities is evolutionarily-ancient (Englemman et al., 2021; 2023; c.f. Redshaw et al., 2016; Suddendorf et al., 2017) and early emerging in ontogeny, and therefore detectable in the behaviors of young infants (e.g., Cesana-Arlotti, 2018; 2022; Téglás & Bonatti, 2016).

Consistent with the minimal representations hypothesis, non-verbal tests of children's modal representations reveal a failure to represent multiple simultaneous possibilities until age 4 (Beck et al., 2006; Leahy, 2023; 2024; 2026; Leahy et al. 2022; Mody & Carey, 2016).

What children cannot do, on this view, is entertain more than one mutually exclusive possibility at a time: that a reward could be located in either of the cups on the two-cup side.

These authors reasoned that if children are able to represent multiple possible outcomes, they should choose to cover both ends of the Y-shaped tube by placing one hand under each.

However, if they fail to represent multiple possibilities, in keeping with the minimal representations hypothesis, they should place just one hand under the opening where they expect the marble to emerge.

Using this method, Redshaw and Suddendorf found that although most 2-year-olds used one hand on every trial, many 3-year-olds used two hands on every trial (39%), or successfully switched to two-handed responses after using one hand for a few trials (33%), while most 4-year-olds (78%) used two hands spontaneously.

text.text: Leahy reasoned that (1) a child who deploys possibility concepts should cover both exits of the Y-shaped tube, (2) a child using minimal representations of possibility should cover one possible exit of the Y-shaped tube; and (3) a child who is not reasoning about possibility in the task, and who fails to evaluate the structure of the apparatus should also frequently cover the impossible exit.
However, in their study, only 17% of 3-year-olds placed a hand under both exits of the Y-shaped tube, suggesting that very few, if any, 3-year-olds deployed possibility concepts.

Further, Leahy found that when children were tested with a "U-shaped tube" (Figure 2c), where only one of two openings was a possible candidate for the ball to exit, 3-year-olds deployed one hand to cover the single possible exit just as often (42%) as they used a two-hand strategy to cover both exits (37%), even though the second exit was physically impossible.

text.text: Given these findings, Leahy argued that 3-year-olds' apparent success on previous iterations of the Y-shaped tubes may have overestimated children's modal reasoning abilities.
In the present study, we challenge two key assumptions of this past work to provide a stronger test of the minimal representations hypothesis.
First, a critical assumption in Leahy's (2024) study was that the impossible tubes he presented were perceived by children as categorically impossible.
text.formatted: First, a critical assumption in <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Leahy's (2024)</ref> study was that the impossible tubes he presented were perceived by children as categorically impossible.

text.text: However, it's unclear that this was the case, since in each of the reported studies the "impossible" distractor tubes were still physically connected to the target "possible" tubes, making it ambiguous whether balls might indeed enter them.

For example, in Leahy's adapted Y-shaped tube, the child was required to infer that the distractor tube was impossible by reasoning that a ball placed into the apparatus would need to travel against gravity to enter it.
Similarly, in the U-tube trials, it was crucial that children notice, as adults might, that for a ball to exit the impossible tube it would have to travel along a path that defies gravity.

However, if children did not reason like adults, or did not attend carefully to the precise location of the entry point, they may have failed to notice this physical impossibility, raising the possibility that their placement of two hands did indeed reflect modal reasoning.

Second, a key challenge to evaluating previous studies using the tubes method, including Leahy's, is that success requires not only modal reasoning, but also a shared understanding of the goals of the game.

For example, rather than thinking that their goal is to maximize the number of objects that they can catch, children may instead understand the task as a test of whether they can correctly guess an object's location.
These two goals should produce very different patterns of behavior, with the first predicting the use of two hands, but the second predicting the placement of one hand under the child's "best bet".
By analogy, whereas one might place bets on all horses in a race to communicate that all outcomes are possible, to win at the races one ordinarily picks a winner and places a single bet.
Similarly, some children may not choose to use two hands because they view their goal as correctly guessing each object's location, not maximizing the number of objects retrieved.

More broadly, existing versions of the tube task do not clearly differentiate between the ability to represent multiple possibilities and the ability to infer the goals of the task and the strategies that are required to succeed.

Given this, failures in previous paradigms may not reflect an inability to represent multiple possibilities, but instead uncertainty about how to act on those representations within the context of a task.
In the present study, we addressed these concerns by making two critical changes to the tube task.

First, we reasoned that a stronger test of Leahy's claim requires making the impossible tubes obviously and categorically impossible -i.e., that there is no reason to make their impossibility ambiguous by connecting them to the possible tubes, as he did, and that introducing this ambiguity undermines the assumption that children perceive them as truly impossible.
Therefore in the two studies we present below, all impossible tubes were obviously impossible.

In particular, we presented children with a Y-shaped tube that was attached to a sheet of perforated pegboard, next to a singleton "impossible" tube that was connected to the apparatus, but not directly connected to the Y-shaped tube (contrary to Leahy, 2024).

Second, and critical to our intervention, we required children to always make two choices at two distinct locations, in order to test which of the three locations they thought were most likely to contain objects.

Specifically, instead of asking children to use their hands to catch dropping balls, they were asked to identify two boxes they wanted to look inside by placing one sticker on each of two locations prior to opening either.

In the familiarization phase, participants were introduced to the apparatus: "We're going to play a game!
Let me show you how it works.
Look, these tubes are connected to some boxes.

The experimenter then dropped a ball down the singleton tube and said, "Look!

When I drop a ball down this tube, it didn't fall here, [E shows empty box], it's here!

This demonstration was completed twice, with the ball falling down the left side once, and the right side once, counterbalanced between participants.

In Study 2, we sought to replicate the pattern of findings in Study 1, while addressing the possibility that older children adopted a heuristic of always choosing both ends of the Y-shaped tube when that response was expected on a large number of trials.

To address this, in Study 2 we tested children with an equal number of trials in which the correct answer was (a) both ends of the Y-shaped tube (critical), or (b) the singleton tube plus one of the two Y-shaped tube locations (two-ball).

We reasoned that if children are minimal representers and only succeed by adopting a heuristic of picking both exits of the Y-shaped tube on all trials with two stickers, then they should again show a preference for both ends of the Y-shaped tube regardless of which locations are the correct choice.
However, if they reason about possibility, then given this balanced trial structure children should only select both exits of the Y-shaped tube when these are the correct choices.

The initial side was counterbalanced between participants, such that half of the children began with the singleton tube on the left side first, and the other half began with it on the right side first.
Third, the test phase began either with a critical trial first or with a two-ball trial first, counterbalanced across participants.

This meant that participants completed the test phase in one of two orders: (1) critical, S-filler, two-ball, Y-filler, critical, S-filler, two-ball, Y-filler, critical, S-filler, two-ball, or (2) two-ball, S-filler, critical, Y-filler, two-ball, S-filler, critical, Y-filler, two-ball, S-filler, critical.

Third, we examined differences in children's accuracy on the Y-filler and S-filler trials, and found no difference between younger and older children (B = -91, n.s.).

We also found no difference in trial_type (B = 1.01, n.s.), nor an age x trial_type interaction (B = 0.85, n.s.), suggesting that although children were more accurate on Y-filler trials than S-filler trials in raw proportion, this did not reflect a systematic preference for the Y-shaped tube over the singleton tube.

Still, to account for the possibility that children might have a generalized preference for the Y-shaped tube, we repeated our main analyses in the subset of older children who were accurate on at least 2/3 S-filler trials (n = 35) and found that these children remained significantly better than chance on critical trials (B =2.59, p = 0.0002).
Taken together, these data suggest that although some children made errors, these decreased with age, and children generally evaluated the structure of the tubes correctly.
We tested the hypothesis that 2-to 3-year-olds deploy "minimal representations" of possibility in the Tubes task using an adaptation of Leahy (2024).

text.text: In two studies, we asked children to identify two locations for a reward.
In Study 1, we found that older children (between 2;7 and 3;2 years of age) -but not younger children -chose the two possible locations most of the time.
In Study 2, both older and younger children (between 2;0 and 2;6) performed better than chance when a more balanced trial structure was used.
Thus, when required to make two choices, children preferred the two exits of the Y-shaped tube over the singleton tube.
This suggests that children thought that both exits of the Y-shaped tube were possible in a way that the singleton tube was not.
Crucially, on the minimal representations view, once a child commits to an object's location, they should consider all remaining locations to be impossible.

The theory therefore predicts no differentiation between locations that are deemed impossible by inference (e.g., the other exit of the Y-shaped tube) and those that are physically impossible (e.g., the singleton).

Although we found considerable variability in the performance of 24-to 30-month-olds, our data suggest that children as young as 2½ (31 months and older) treated physically possible outcomes differently from a physically impossible outcome, contrary to Leahy's (2024) findings, and consistent with the idea that children can reason about multiple distinct possibilities.

text.text: Was children's reasoning in our study based on modal reasoning, or did they differentiate possible from impossible outcomes using sequential simulation?

As described in the Introduction, Leahy and colleagues (Leahy et al., 2022; Leahy, 2024) argued that children show greater success on past versions of the Tubes task because they sequentially simulated the possible locations of the reward -e.g., first imagining one possible location but not the other, and then, when given feedback that their choice was incorrect, imagining the second possible location.
text.formatted: As described in the Introduction, Leahy and colleagues <ref type="bibr">(Leahy et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Leahy, 2024)</ref> argued that children show greater success on past versions of the Tubes task because they sequentially simulated the possible locations of the reward -e.g., first imagining one possible location but not the other, and then, when given feedback that their choice was incorrect, imagining the second possible location.

text.text: Given this, a key goal of the present study was to minimize the likelihood of sequential simulation by asking children to simultaneously identify two possible locations of a reward without knowing the outcome of either location.
To accomplish this, on critical trials the experimenter handed the child two stickers together, and trained them to place both stickers on two boxes at the same time.
On these trials, the child did not receive feedback from the experimenter regarding the actual object locations before both stickers were placed.

Thus, although it remains possible that children engage in sequential simulation when they are forced to make two simultaneous choices, this would require that they do so quickly, either before making their choices or during the response process.

Crucially, this would make sequential simulation difficult to empirically differentiate from a simultaneous process that reflects modal reasoning in any age group, including 4-year-olds, whose success on such tasks has been argued to reflect modal reasoning (e.g., Carey, 2020; Leahy et al., 2022; Leahy, 2026).

text.text: Another way to explain our findings is to argue that children assigned a different status to "physical" vs. "inferred" impossibility.

We reasoned, following the minimal representation view, that once a child commits to a particular object location all other locations become impossible, and equally so, predicting no difference between them.
However, could it be the case that children treat physical impossibility as more impossible than inferred impossibility?
Two versions of this hypothesis might be proposed.
First, children might completely ignore the singleton tube, and have a generalized bias to select exits of the Y-shaped tube regardless of the ball locations.
Against this, however, children almost always chose the singleton tube exit when appropriate.
Also, our main results remained significant when excluding children who showed any sign of a Y-shaped tube bias.
A second possibility is that children might have a graded notion of impossibility, classifying physically impossible tubes as more impossible than tubes that are deemed impossible by inference.

The problem with this view is that there is no clear sense in which something can be partially impossible without being partially possible, and in general, impossibility is treated as absolute in modal logic.

For example, while previous accounts argue for graded notions of possibility (Kratzer, 1981; Lassiter, 2017), and recognize different varieties of necessity (Fine, 2005), they never assign gradations of possibility to impossible events.

text.text: Interestingly, some accounts posit gradations of similarity between possible and impossible worlds (Nolan, 1997), potentially explaining human judgments that levitating a feather might be easier than levitating a rock (e.g., Shtulman & Morgan, 2017;  for related studies, see Hu et al., 2026; Khan & Starmans, 2025).

text.text: However, even on these accounts, logically impossible worlds remain categorically impossible.

Just as important, multiple empirical studies with older children suggest that rather than having a more fine-grained understanding of impossibility than adults (e.g., that might allow them to assign some impossible events a gradient of possibility), children instead have a tendency to categorize improbable events as categorically impossible.

For example, many 4-to 5-year-olds judge that it's impossible to find a crocodile under their bed or to make pickle-flavoured ice-cream, though both are possible and differ only in probability (e.g., Goulding & Freidman, 2021; Shtulman & Carey, 2007; also see Hu et al., 2026; Khan &   Starmans, 2025).

text.text: The results of this study are relevant to the claim that children's ability to reason about multiple possibilities is tied to their acquisition of modal language.

In past studies, proponents of the minimal representations hypothesis have argued that children begin to succeed on tests of modal reasoning at 4 years of age owing to their acquisition of modal language (see Leahy & Carey, 2026; Leahy & Zalnieriunas, 2022;  for relevant discussion, also see: Dieuleveut & van Dooren, 2025), and 3-year-olds fail to reason about possibility because they have not yet acquired modal language (Mody & Carey, 2016; Leahy et al., 2020; 2022; Leahy, 2024; 2026; Leahy & Zalnieriunas, 2022).

text.text: Our finding that children may succeed by age 2½ conflicts with this conclusion.
In particular, our data suggest that many children can simultaneously represent multiple possible locations of a reward before they comprehend modal language.
Therefore, it's possible that rather than driving the development of modal concepts, modal language may emerge only once non-verbal possibility concepts have emerged in development.
Although our findings suggest that 2½-year-olds may be able to represent multiple possibilities simultaneously, they also leave open a number of questions that should be addressed in future studies.
First, although older children between 2;7 and 3;2 years were consistently successful across both studies, younger children between 2;0 and 2;6 were much more variable in their performance.
One possibility is that younger children are more likely to perseverate over a specific strategy and gradually become better at understanding the goals of the task.
Future research should further explore the mechanisms underlying younger children's behaviour using other, arguably more sensitive measures of children's reasoning.

Second, although our study suggests that strategy choice and planning may obscure modal reasoning in the Y-shaped tube task, it's unclear whether a similar explanation can be deployed to explain failures on other tasks, or if distinct explanations are required.
Future studies should consider constructing a cups task analogous to the task used here, but that makes clearer the goal of optimizing reward vs.
exploration.

Finally, because we were unable to collect demographic data about our participants' socioeconomic status or ethnic backgrounds, it's possible that these demographic factors -or co-occurring differences in executive functioning or vocabulary -explain some variability in our data, and therefore limit the generalizability of these findings.
Future research should explore these questions.

In the present studies, we tested the minimal representations hypothesis by requiring children to always make two choices from three available options, and found that children as young as 2½ were able to make possibility inferences when given a clear goal of maximizing their rewards.
Children's ability to choose two merely possible locations for a reward while avoiding the impossible location is most compatible with simultaneous representations of possibility.
